C. T. 2008. ?network: a Package for Managing Relational Data in R.? Journal

'Edge list: This must consist of a rectangular matrix or two-dimensional
array whose row
elements represent edges. The i; 1st cell of this structure is taken to be
the ID of the

head vertex. (Only dyadic networks may be input in this fashion.)

if present, are taken to contain edge attribute values.** The matrix.type

crnet<-network(cr,directed=F,matrix.type='edgelist',ignore.eval=FALSE,names.eval='publication_count')

aware that building networks with non-numeric edgelists was even

messages.subject: [statnet_help] using ergm on large networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Juan,

The problem here is that you are using the receiver term, which adds a
parameter for every node (but one), so you are trying to fit a model
with ~9000 parameters. The MPLE procedure tries to allocate a vector to
store all of them --- which is 9000*MPLE.max.dyad.types, which, by
default, asks for a vector about 9e+9*8 = 72 gigabytes in length.

Setting MPLE.max.dyad.types to too small a value means that the MPLE
procedure cannot run, resulting in the "Too many unique dyad values"
error.

In other words, the problem is not so much that the network is too big,
but that the model calls for too many parameters. My recommendation is
to try modeling degree heterogeneity in some other way (e.g., using
gwidegree).

                        I hope this helps,
                        Pavel

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 14 Feb 2013, Juan Pablo Alperin wrote:

> So, let me ask: what is the right way to model a network that has a power-law degree
> distribution? Is gwidegree the only type of preferential attachment model currently
> possible?

A better question might be how to use ergm to *test* whether a 
network has a power-law degree distribution.

There's a paper you might want to look at on this exact topic:


Degree distributions in sexual networks: a framework for evaluating 
evidence.
Hamilton DT, Handcock MS, Morris M.
Sex Transm Dis. 2008 Jan;35(1):30-40.

Mark Handcock has made the code available in a CRAN package called 
"degreenet".

best,
mm

> I will follow-up on the other issue in the other thread. Thanks.
> 
> Juan
> 
> On Thursday, 14 February, 2013 at 12:13 AM, Pavel N. Krivitsky wrote:
>
>       Hi, Juan,
> 
> The problem here is that you are using the receiver term, which adds a
> parameter for every node (but one), so you are trying to fit a model
> with ~9000 parameters. The MPLE procedure tries to allocate a vector to
> store all of them --- which is 9000*MPLE.max.dyad.types, which, by
> default, asks for a vector about 9e+9*8 = 72 gigabytes in length.
> 
> Setting MPLE.max.dyad.types to too small a value means that the MPLE
> procedure cannot run, resulting in the "Too many unique dyad values"
> error.
> 
> In other words, the problem is not so much that the network is too big,
> but that the model calls for too many parameters. My recommendation is
> to try modeling degree heterogeneity in some other way (e.g., using
> gwidegree).
> 
> I hope this helps,
> Pavel
> 
> On Fri, 2013-02-08 at 21:26 -0800, Juan Pablo Alperin wrote:
>       Hello all,
>

> models. I have a network with ~9000 nodes, but even when I try to run

>

>

> to what is happening?
> 
> A follow-up question: I've read of difficulties fitting ergm's to
> large networks. Does anyone have a good resource or a set of tips on
> working with ergms on large networks?
> 
> Really hope someone can help. Thanks!
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] meta analysis for ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ya,

The R package hergm is trying to do something more complicated than you
want, although it could be adapted to multilevel analysis.
The R package RSiena aka Siena 4 cannot handle cross-sectional data, but
Siena 3 and multilevel p2 could.

hergm is trying to do something more complicated than you want:
whereas in multilevel analysis you may have, e.g., students nested in
schools and you know which student is nested in which school, hergm
assumes that you do not know which node (e.g., student) belongs to which
subset of nodes (e.g., school).
It attempts to learn the memberships of nodes to subsets of nodes from the
observed network (under some assumptions on the data-generating process).
However, hergm could be adapted to multilevel analysis.
I would be happy to do so, but I have been traveling a lot lately and I
cannot do it in the near future.

RSiena aka Siena 4 deals with longitudinal network data.
If you have cross-sectional data, you cannot use Siena 4, but you could
use Siena 3, which allows you to do meta-analysis.
Siena 3 is no longer maintained, but you can find it here:
http://www.gmw.rug.nl/~stocnet/StOCNET.htm

An alternative would be the multilevel p2 model of Bonne Zijlstra
(B.J.H.Zijlstra@uva.nl) and Marijtje van Duijn (m.a.j.van.duijn@rug.nl).
The multilevel p2 model, as the name suggests, is a multilevel model and
therefore preferable to the meta-analytic approach of Siena 3.
But the downside is that it assumes dyad-independence:
http://www.gmw.rug.nl/~stocnet/StOCNET.htm

Hope this helps,
Michael
